title: Parallelism on CPU
blurb: Tests how the GIL decides between threading and multiprocessing, why threads stay flat on CPU-bound work but scale on I/O, the cost of process pools and where to create them, joblib's overhead, and how many workers to use for I/O.

questions.explanation: It serialises bytecode within one interpreter. It is released during I/O waits and some C-extension calls, which is why threads still help for I/O.

questions.prompt: Why does multiprocessing get real CPU parallelism when threading doesn't?
options: Processes share one GIL but take turns much faster than threads do.
Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL.
Processes run Python bytecode on the GPU.
The GIL only exists in the main process.
questions.explanation: Separate interpreters run truly in parallel on separate cores, at the cost of spawning processes and serialising data between them.

questions.prompt: With 8 threads on CPU-bound work, what speedup did the chapter measure?
options: About 7x, close to linear
Below 0.5x, slower than running on a single thread
About 1.0x, flat at every thread count
About 4x, half of ideal
questions.explanation: The flat line is the GIL's signature. Threads never gave real CPU parallelism at any count. Processes reached 7.24x.

refLinks.label: §53.2.1 CPU-Bound: The GIL Makes Threading Flat, Multiprocessing Scale

questions.prompt: At 8 workers, threads took 2.631 s and processes 0.362 s on the same work. How many times faster were processes? Give one decimal place.
What does Procedure 53.2 say about where to create the process pool?
options: Once per batch, so each batch gets fresh workers
Once, outside any loop, and reuse it for all the work
Only after timing starts, so creation counts in the benchmark
Inside the worker function, so each task has its own pool
questions.explanation: Process creation is a fixed cost. Creating pools inside a loop was 96x slower than not parallelising at all for small tasks.

questions.prompt: Why do threads scale well on I/O-bound work like network calls?
options: The GIL is released while a thread waits, so waits overlap.
The operating system quietly merges all the calls into one request.
I/O work runs on a separate core that has no GIL.
Threads cache the network responses for each other.
questions.explanation: time.sleep, socket reads and disk reads all release the GIL while blocked. Threads reached 7.95x at 8 workers.

refLinks.label: §53.2.2 I/O-Bound: The Opposite Result, Equally Real

questions.prompt: Threads and processes scaled about equally on the sleep test. Why does the chapter still prefer threads for I/O?
options: Processes can't do I/O while the GIL is held
Threads are always faster than processes for any workload
Same scaling, less overhead
Threads use the GPU for network calls
questions.explanation: With equal scaling, the cheaper tool wins. Threads also share memory without serialisation.

refLinks.label: §53.2.2 I/O-Bound: The Opposite Result, Equally Real

questions.prompt: An I/O-bound job runs on a 16-core machine. What does Procedure 53.3 say about thread count?
options: It should be half the cores, to leave room for the OS.
It should be 1, since the GIL allows only one thread.
It can exceed 16, since threads mostly wait.
It must stay at 16, one thread per core.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake is capping I/O threads at the core count. Waiting threads don't need a core.

questions.prompt: Creating and tearing down a pool for tiny tasks took 11.3 ms per iteration, against 0.12 ms serially. About how many times slower was the pool? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 11.3 / 0.12 = 94 with these rounded figures. The book reports 96x from the unrounded timings. Either way, the fixed cost of processes swamps tiny work.

questions.prompt: What makes process-pool creation expensive regardless of the work?
options: Starting and stopping processes and interpreters
Allocating GPU memory for every worker
Compiling the worker function for each process
Copying the whole GIL into each process
questions.explanation: Forking or spawning a process and starting an interpreter is a fixed cost, independent of task size. Small tasks can't amortise it.

questions.prompt: joblib.Parallel was about 33% slower than raw multiprocessing.Pool. What does that buy?
options: Nothing. It is a measurement artefact.
Robustness, such as crash handling
GPU offload for scikit-learn models
Thread-based execution that avoids the GIL
questions.explanation: The overhead is real and pays for reliability and a convenient API. Use raw multiprocessing for a controlled hot path, joblib where robustness matters.

questions.prompt: Raw multiprocessing took 0.387 s and joblib 0.515 s. What percentage slower was joblib? Give a whole number.
What single question does Procedure 53.1 use to pick threading or multiprocessing?
options: Does the work spend its time computing or waiting?
Does the data fit in the L3 cache?
How many CPU cores does the machine it runs on have?
Is the code written with async and await?
questions.explanation: Computing means multiprocessing. Waiting means threading. Core count matters later, for how many workers.

questions.prompt: How does asyncio differ from threading for I/O-bound work, per the chapter?
options: Many processes, each with its own event loop
It removes the GIL for the duration of each request
One thread, cooperative scheduling, async libraries
It runs CPU-bound code in parallel on all cores
questions.explanation: asyncio avoids OS thread switching but needs async/await-aware libraries. It solves the same I/O problem, not CPU parallelism.

questions.prompt: A pipeline resizes 50,000 images in pure Python (CPU-bound), then uploads each to object storage (I/O-bound). Which plan fits the chapter?
options: A single thread for both stages, since the GIL serialises everything anyway
Threads for both stages, since they share memory
A process pool for resizing, created once, then a thread pool for uploads
Processes for both, with one new pool per image
questions.explanation: Match each stage to its bound: processes for computing, threads for waiting, pools created once. A pool per image pays the fixed cost 50,000 times.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why threading gives a flat ~1.0x "speedup" for CPU-bound work regardless of thread count, while multiprocessing scales close to linearly for the identical workload. Name the specific mechanism responsible.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time per process; for CPU-bound work, threads spend essentially all their time wanting to execute bytecode, so they end up serialised regardless of thread count, producing the flat ~1.0-1.1x result. Multiprocessing uses separate OS processes, each with its own interpreter and own GIL, so CPU-bound work genuinely runs concurrently across cores, hence the near-linear scaling.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "threads are always lighter-weight than processes, so I should default to threading." Using this chapter's I/O-bound and CPU-bound results, write two or three sentences explaining why the right default depends on the workload, not on thread weight alone.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Threads are indeed lighter-weight to create than processes, but "lighter-weight" only matters for I/O-bound work, where the GIL is released during waits and threads' low overhead pays off directly (this chapter's I/O-bound results show threading scaling as well as multiprocessing, with less overhead). For CPU-bound work, the GIL makes threading's lightness irrelevant. It still caps effective concurrency at ~1x regardless of overhead, so multiprocessing is required despite its heavier cost.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 53.1's decision rule, classify each of the following as CPU-bound or I/O-bound and name the right tool: (a) resizing 10,000 images; (b) fetching data from 200 REST API endpoints; (c) computing a large matrix decomposition; (d) reading 500 files from a slow network filesystem.

Using Procedure 53.2, rewrite a function that currently creates a fresh `multiprocessing.Pool` inside a loop processing 100 batches of work, so that the pool is created once. Using this chapter's measured 96x pool-creation overhead, estimate the rough time saved if each batch's real work takes 5ms.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Using the chapter's measured ~96x pool-creation overhead: creating a fresh pool per batch costs roughly 96x what the real 5ms of work alone would cost, i.e. close to 480ms per batch instead of ~5ms-plus-negligible-reused-pool-overhead. Across 100 batches, that's roughly (480ms - 5ms) × 100 ≈ 47.5 seconds of pure avoidable overhead eliminated by creating the pool once outside the loop.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured `joblib` at 33% slower than raw `multiprocessing.Pool`, while the reference material for this workload elsewhere reports figures closer to 48% on a different run. Propose a methodological reason two honest measurements of the same comparison could differ by this much, referencing Chapter 48's benchmarking discipline.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Benchmarking discipline (Chapter 48) requires warm-up and repeated measurement with reported medians, not single runs. Two "honest" measurements can differ this much if one run included cold-start effects, differing background system load, thermal throttling, or a different number of repetitions/warm-up iterations. Without knowing both measurements' exact benchmarking methodology, an 48%-vs-33% discrepancy is exactly the kind of gap Chapter 48 warns single or poorly-controlled measurements can produce.

bookExercises.prompt: A team is building a web scraper that both parses large HTML documents (CPU-bound) and issues many HTTP requests (I/O-bound) as part of the same pipeline. Propose an architecture using both `threading` and `multiprocessing` appropriately, and justify which stage uses which.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Architecture: use `ThreadPoolExecutor` for the I/O-bound HTTP-fetching stage (many concurrent requests, GIL released during network waits) feeding results into a `ProcessPoolExecutor` for the CPU-bound HTML-parsing stage (genuine multi-core parallelism needed since parsing keeps the GIL busy). Threads handle the waiting-dominated stage; processes handle the compute-dominated stage, matching each stage's bottleneck to the tool built for it.

bookExercises.prompt: Read enough of PEP 703 to summarize, in a few sentences, what a "no-GIL" CPython build changes about this chapter's central threading-vs-multiprocessing result. Would the flat ~1.0x threading result for CPU-bound work still be expected under a no-GIL build?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. PEP 703 proposes making the GIL optional, allowing true multi-threaded parallelism for CPU-bound Python code. Under a no-GIL build, this chapter's flat ~1.0x threading result for CPU-bound work would NOT be expected to hold. Threads would be able to execute bytecode genuinely concurrently across cores, and threading should scale similarly to multiprocessing for CPU-bound work, without multiprocessing's process-spawn and serialization overhead.

bookExercises.prompt: Watch or read a summary of Beazley's "Understanding the Python GIL" talk. Identify one GIL-related behavior it covers that this chapter does not (for example, GIL contention patterns between many threads doing a mix of CPU and I/O work), and explain how it would affect the "prefer threading for I/O-bound work" recommendation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. GIL contention patterns for threads mixing CPU and I/O work within the same pool is a common topic Beazley's talk covers that this chapter's clean CPU-bound/I/O-bound split does not. Real workloads are often a mix, and contention between threads competing for the GIL when some are CPU-heavy can degrade the I/O-bound threads' apparent scaling too. This would complicate the "prefer threading for I/O-bound work" recommendation whenever I/O-bound threads share a process with any CPU-heavy work, suggesting the clean recommendation applies most cleanly to workloads that are purely one or the other.
